newsitem.title: JAPAN: DOLLAR FIRMER BUT TRIMS GAINS BY LATE TOKYO.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR FIRMER BUT TRIMS GAINS BY LATE TOKYO.

text.p: 0646 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar was firmer against the yen by late Tokyo on Monday after Japanese investors, importers and U.S. operators bought back the greenback after its nearly four yen drop in overseas trade on Friday, dealers said.
But speculative sales in the afternoon trimmed the dollar's earlier gains after its upside was confirmed to be heavy. Falls in Japanese share prices had only a limited impact.
"Japanese importers have been very eager to buy dollars all day today. Some of our clients called us from home to buy the greenback although they are on summer holidays," a city bank dealer said.
Japanese life insurers, securities houses, oil companies, trust banks and U.S. fund operators were also said to be behind the dollar's recovery above 115 yen in morning trade.

But a lack of follow-through purchases and a market rumour that a Chinese bank was placing offers limited the dollar's advance above 115.60 yen, triggering fresh sales by interbank dealers and speculators, dealers said.
The yen's continued strength against major currencies in crosses also indirectly weighed on the dollar versus the yen.
The mark was at 62.18/23 yen and sterling stood at around 182.56/68 yen at 0710 GMT, compared with 62.22 yen and 182.25 yen respectively at Friday's New York close.
Currency dealers mostly shrugged off a steep fall in the Japanese stock market.

The Tokyo stock market's benchmark Nikkei average tumbled nearly four percent on Monday to close at its lowest level since April 28, hurt by the dollar's tumble against the yen and a slide on Wall Street on Friday, brokers said.
The Nikkei 225 plunged 780.28 points or 3.98 percent to 18,824.18, racking up its largest point loss of calendar 1997.

The market was, however, closely watching U.S. stock and bond markets to see whether the downward trend would continue later in New York trade after a heavy selloff in U.S. stock and bond markets compounded the dollar's woes in New York on Friday, dealers said.

"The key point (for currency markets) will be how far U.S. asset markets, such as stocks and bonds, will face further corrective sales in the future," said Nobuya Shida, manager of the trading division at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
Another wave of sales in U.S. stock and bond markets could prompt further dollar selling, dealers said.
But they said the dollar is not likely to quickly fall to the 110-yen level seen in May because there has been no significant change in the United States' strong fundamentals.

The dollar pared part of its heavy losses on Friday against the mark, but remained vulnerable in Tokyo. Dealers said the technical trend of the dollar could become weaker should it fall below 1.8410/20 marks again. The dollar closed at 114.75/85 yen and 1.8450/60 marks in New York on Friday.
